paper_title: Manga2Animate: An Agentic Framework for Faithful Manga Animation with Script and Storyboard Planning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Adapting existing manga into coherent animation that stays faithful to the source is a valuable yet challenging task. Existing methods either access the manga mainly through text, losing its characters and art style, or feed manga pages directly into video generation models, which misinterpret the manga's structure and produce incorrect storylines. In this paper, we propose Manga2Animate, a multi-agent framework that grounds every stage of generation in the source manga. We decompose the task into two intermediate representations, an animation script and a visual storyboard. Each representation is produced by a creator agent and reviewed against the source panels by a paired reviewer agent. We tailor representation-specific selection and dual-level feedback to progressively refine both before synthesizing the final animation. Extensive experiments and a user study demonstrate that Manga2Animate produces animations more faithful to the source manga and more consistent across shots than state-of-the-art approaches. Project page: https://annchenn.github.io/Manga2Animate/

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Manga is one of the richest sources of stories for animation. Popular titles are routinely adapted into anime, and fans expect these adaptations to move smoothly and tell the story coherently while Equal contribution. 1 Preprint. Under review. Figure 2: Limitations of existing methods to manga-to-animation generation. (a) Text-based storytelling methods (AniMaker, ViMax, StoryMem) access the manga mainly through text, losing its art style ( 1 ) or distorting characters ( 2 ). (b) Feeding manga pages into video model (e.g., Seedance 2.0) tells the wrong story ( 3 ) and shows manga panels as video frames ( 4 ). remaining faithful to the characters and art style they love. Yet producing such an adaptation remains slow and costly, often taking large teams of artists months of storyboarding, key animation, inbetweening, and coloring. At the same time, manga already specifies much of what an animation needs, including who the characters are and what they look like, how each shot is framed, and how the plot unfolds. With recent advances in video generation, it is natural to ask whether manga can be brought to life automatically. However, as Fig. 2 shows, storytelling systems that first describe the manga in words discard its visual appearance, so the original art style is lost ( 1 ) and characters change appearance or drift between anime and photorealistic styles ( 2 ). Feeding manga pages directly into video model fails for different reason. The model knows neither the order in which the panels should be read nor what speech balloons mean, so it tells the wrong story ( 3 ) or even places manga panels, or entire pages, directly into the video as frames ( 4 ). Our key observation is that todays video generation models already know how to animate. What they cannot do is understand manga. Given manga page, they produce smooth and appealing motion, yet they follow the panels in the wrong order and misread the speech balloons, so the result looks convincing but tells completely wrong story (Fig. 2b). We therefore do not replace these models. Instead, we keep their rich visual knowledge and give them what they are missing, clear understanding of the manga. Much like an animation studio, Manga2Animate  (Fig. 1)  first turns the manga into an animation script, which describes what happens in each panel, and storyboard, which shows how each shot should look. Both are built by AI agents and checked against the original panels, so the video model receives faithful plan instead of raw manga pages. We find that this plan effectively constrains generation. With the script fixing the plot and the storyboard fixing the characters, composition, and art style, the video model no longer has to interpret the manga on its own and can focus on what it does best, bringing the story to life. Experiments show that Manga2Animate produces animations that are more faithful to the original characters, art style, and plot than existing storytelling and video generation methods, even when these methods are given the same script as ours. Because our framework guides existing models rather than replacing them, it works with both open-source and commercial image and video generators, and outperforms prior methods with either. In user study, participants selected our results as the best overall in over 90% of responses, for both storyboards and videos. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We present Manga2Animate, to the best of our knowledge the first automated framework that turns existing manga into animation that is faithful to source manga. 2 Preprint. Under review. We show that planning through script and storyboard, iteratively refined with duallevel feedback from both and verified against the original manga, is key to preserving the characters, art style, and plot. We establish an evaluation protocol for manga-to-animation generation, under which Manga2Animate outperforms existing methods, and we further validate these results with user study.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Manga understanding. Built on annotated corpora (Matsui et al., 2017; Aizawa et al., 2020; Vivoli et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024a), manga understanding has progressed from detecting panels, characters, and text (Shen et al., 2023) to ordering panels and attributing dialogue (Sachdeva & Zisserman, 2024), naming characters across chapters (Sachdeva et al., 2024), and narrating chapters as prose (Sachdeva & Zisserman, 2025). Vision-language models are now benchmarked on manga (Baek et al., 2026; Ikuta et al., 2025; Vivoli et al., 2025), yet still misread cross-panel narrative (Baranwal et al., 2025) and can rely on memorized popular content rather than visual evidence (Szu-Tu et al., 2025); generation from comics remains largely unexplored (Vivoli et al., 2024b). We use Sachdeva & Zisserman (2024) for pre-processing and, given this fragility, review every intermediate output against the source panels. Story visualization. Story visualization renders narrative as consistent image sequence, evolving from GANs (Li et al., 2019) to diffusion models with visual memory (Rahman et al., 2023), identity conditioning (Ye et al., 2023), shared attention (Tewel et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024), frame context (Liu et al., 2024a), multi-subject personalization (He et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2025b), iterative refinement (Mao et al., 2026), and language-model layout planning (He et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2024), with dedicated benchmarks (Zhuang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2025) and extensions to manga generation (Wu et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026a). These methods generate from text, whereas our storyboard is conditioned on and selected against the manga panels. Multi-shot video generation. Video diffusion has advanced from short clips (Ho et al., 2022) to foundation models (Kong et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Polyak et al., 2024; Seedance et al., 2026), whose adherence to explicit specifications is now benchmarked (Huang et al., 2026d). Cross-shot consistency is pursued through long-context tuning (Guo et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026), keyframe memory (Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2026), storyboard anchoring (Zhang et al., 2026), and reference-based identity injection (Jiang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Hu et al., 2025). For animation, anime-oriented models and datasets (Jiang et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025) and in-betweening and colorization methods (Xing et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b; Tang et al., 2025) create motion and color from sparse inputs. We use such models as interchangeable backends and, in the spirit of decoupling explicit state from generative rendering (Huang et al., 2026c), obtain consistency from the reviewed script and storyboard rather than from architecture (Sec. 4.4). Agentic storytelling video generation. Language and vision-language agents increasingly orchestrate video production from script to storyboard, clips, and assembly (Lin et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b; Xu et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025c; Hu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026b), some with critics that select clips by tree search (Shi et al., 2025), gate anime production stages (Zhang et al., 2025b; Yan et al., 2026), or self-improve at test time (Long et al., 2026), following self-feedback in language agents (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023), pattern also adopted to verify generated images and figures (Huang et al., 2026a; Tseng et al., 2026). Our creatorreviewer design is closest to these systems, but they invent characters, shots, and plot from prompt and can only check outputs against their own script, whereas our reviewers check against the manga panels. Earlier manga-to-animation systems only moved virtual camera over panels or added synthesized speech (Cao et al., 2016; Gupta et al., 2021); to our knowledge, ours is the first to generate faithful multi-shot animation from manga pages. 3 Preprint. Under review. Figure 3: Overview of the Manga2Animate pipeline. (a) Pre-processing extracts ordered panels, transcript, and character descriptions. (b) Creator and reviewer agents refine an animation script and visual storyboard over rounds and select the best script and best storyboard, dual-level feedback also guides the next round. (c) Video generation runs in first-frame or reference-conditioned mode.

3.1 TASK FORMULATION
Given a set of manga pages M = {m1, . . . , mp} in their original reading order, our goal is to
generate a coherent animated video V . Each manga page consists of multiple manga panels, where
a panel is an individual visual frame depicting a particular moment, action, or scene. From the input
pages, we obtain an ordered sequence of Np target manga panels P = {p1, . . . , pNp } (Np = 6
in our experiments) and a transcript T . For prominent characters appearing in the selected manga
panels, we additionally use character reference images R. These references are taken from official
color artwork when available; otherwise, clear appearances of the characters are cropped from the
input manga.
sections.content: Our pipeline transforms these inputs through two intermediate representations: an animation script = {s1, . . . , sNp } and visual storyboard = {b1, . . . , bNp }, before producing the final video , as illustrated in Fig. 3. We also derive per-character descriptions from the reference images R. The use of and is inspired by real-world animation production workflows, where the narrative is first organized into script and subsequently translated into storyboard before animation is produced. Following this workflow, serves as the textual specification of the animation. Each script clip si describes the content corresponding to manga panel pi, including the scene, camera, character positions and actions, expressions, and dialogue. The storyboard then converts this textual specification into visual plan, where each storyboard panel bi specifies the appearance and scene composition of the corresponding animated clip. Throughout the pipeline, we maintain an explicit correspondence between the source manga and the generated representations as illustrated in Fig. A1: manga panel pi, script clip si, and storyboard panel bi all describe the same narrative unit. This alignment allows each generated component to be directly traced back to its source manga panel during review and refinement.

sections.title: 3.3 PRE-PROCESSING
sections.content: Manga pages often exhibit non-trivial panel layouts, making reading order an important prerequisite for preserving the narrative flow. We therefore detect the panels on each page and determine their reading order using manga-specific detection model and its associated ordering algorithm (Sachdeva & Zisserman, 2024). The resulting ordered panel sequence is then passed to the subsequent stages of the pipeline. In parallel, the same model also detects and transcribes the text on these pages, which we merge into single transcript spanning all pages to help the Script Creator write each panels dialogue and plot (Sec. 3.4). Also, we use Character Description Creator to establish consistent representation of each character from the reference image R. It extracts relatively stable, identity-defining traits, such as facial features and body build, while excluding variable attributes such as clothing and accessories. These character descriptions are then provided to the downstream Script and Storyboard Creators to help maintain character consistency throughout the generation process.

sections.title: 3.4 SCRIPT AND STORYBOARD REFINEMENT
sections.content: To improve generation reliability while controlling API costs, we combine small number of candidates per stage with iterative refinement, in which reviewer feedback guides the next round of generation. We run = 2 refinement rounds: the first round explores initial candidates, and the second round revises them using the first-round feedback. In each refinement round, the Script Creator generates Ns script candidates (Ns = 3) conditioned on the manga panels, character descriptions, transcript, and, from the second round onward, the feedback from the previous round. Errors in scripts are largely local, candidate may describe one panel precisely yet misread another, and different candidates tend to make different mistakes. Selecting single script as whole would discard the correct descriptions contained in the other candidates. The Script Reviewer therefore performs compositional selection at the clip level  (Fig. 4)  , preserving complementary strengths across candidates, and records the remaining weaknesses of each selected component as feedback for the next round. The Storyboard Creator then generates Nb storyboard candidates (Nb = 3) for the selected script. Unlike scripts, closed-source storyboards are selected as complete image because their panels are generated jointly and share style, color, and lighting; recombining panels across candidates could introduce visual inconsistencies. The Storyboard Reviewer compares candidates pairwise in the first round and, in later rounds, compares each new candidate with the previous best, judging each storyboard against the script that produced it. If no new candidate wins, the previous best storyboard 5 Preprint. Under review. is retained with its script and feedback, keeping the final pair consistent. The open-source backend instead generates and selects panels individually before compositing them due to its constraints (more details in Appendix B). Script-level and storyboard-level feedback are jointly provided to the next-round Script Creator, together with the best script from the previous round and the source manga panels. This duallevel feedback allows the pipeline to refine the textual specification using evidence from its visual realization. Issues flagged by the Storyboard Reviewer are treated as symptoms of ambiguous or inaccurate script descriptions: the Script Creator is instructed to identify the responsible part of the script, such as an ambiguous spatial description or missing detail. To prevent unnecessary changes to already correct content, the Script Creator revises only the script clips or character descriptions explicitly identified as problematic by the reviewers, while leaving all other entries unchanged. When feedback from different reviewers conflicts, the corresponding source manga panel is used as the primary reference for deciding the revision. The script and storyboard selected in the final round are then passed to the video-generation stage.

sections.title: 3.5 VIDEO GENERATION PIPELINE
sections.content: To accommodate different input formats of video generation models, our video generation pipeline supports two modes: first-frame mode and reference-conditioned mode. The former is used for models that take single image as the first frame, while the latter is used for models that can take the complete storyboard as reference and generate multi-shot video at once. Our main experimental results use the reference-conditioned mode. In first-frame mode, each storyboard panel serves as the first frame of its corresponding clip. For each clip, the Video Creator generates Nv candidates (Nv = 2) conditioned on that panel and its script description, and the Video Reviewer selects the better one using the script, panel, and previously selected clip when available. This greedy and clip-by-clip process enforces cross-clip continuity at selection time, after which the selected clips are concatenated in story order. In referenceconditioned mode, the Video Creator instead uses the complete best script and full storyboard to generate Nv complete multi-shot candidates in one pass, from which the Video Reviewer selects the final result.

sections.title: 4.1 DATASETS
sections.content: Our evaluation set contains eight stories of six ordered manga panels, drawn from Manga109 (Matsui et al., 2017; Aizawa et al., 2020) and additional cases covering diverse backgrounds, characters, interactions, and actions. All methods use the same stories, enabling evaluation of both panel-level fidelity and cross-clip consistency.

sections.title: 4.2 BASELINES
sections.content: We use StoryDiffusion (Zhou et al., 2024), Story-Iter (Mao et al., 2026), and AnyStory (He et al., 2025b) as storyboard-generation baselines, and AniMaker (Shi et al., 2025), ViMax (Huang et al., 2026b), and StoryMem (Zhang et al., 2025a) as video-generation baselines. We further compare with direct manga-to-video generation by feeding the manga pages directly into Seedance 2.0 or MiniMax-H3. To compare generation ability rather than manga understanding, every script-based baseline receives the same refined script as Manga2Animate. We also provide the same manga character reference images whenever the baseline accepts reference images. Full adaptation details are in Appendix E.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present Manga2Animate, multi-agent framework for faithfully adapting existing manga into coherent multi-shot animation. We decompose the task into two intermediate representations grounded in the source manga, an animation script and visual storyboard. Creator and reviewer agents iteratively generate, review, and refine both. Since the two representations fail in different ways, we compose scripts clip by clip, select storyboards as whole, and feed storyboard-level issues back to the script. Under MangaEval, an evaluation protocol adapted from ViStoryBench and VBench++, Manga2Animate outperforms state-of-the-art storyboard and video generation methods on manga-fidelity and consistency metrics, even when baselines receive the same refined script and character references, and is strongly preferred in user study. Promising future directions include improving robustness to complex or roughly sketched art styles, developing source-grounded evaluation of story events, and extending narrative understanding across pages and chapters. Limitations. Our method has several limitations. First, as an agentic pipeline built on stochastic generative models, its outputs may vary across runs. Second, API-based models may restrict generation of copyrighted or policy-sensitive content. Finally, when the source manga is highly sketchy, cluttered, or compositionally complex, or scene requires context from elsewhere in the story, the pipeline may misinterpret panel content. 9 Preprint. sections.title: APPENDIX
sections.content: This appendix provides additional details that complement the main paper. Sec. describes the implementation details, including model versions, hyperparameters, video specifications, hardware, and cost. Sec. explains the panel-wise generation strategy of the open-source storyboard backend, Sec. reports the storyboard quantitative evaluation, Sec. gives the full script-selection-strategy ablation, the dual-level feedback ablation, an ablation on the refinement loop and storyboard generation, and comparison of reference-conditioned and first-frame video generation, Sec. describes how each baseline is adapted to manga inputs, Sec. gives the full definitions of the MangaEval metrics and our modifications, Sec. summarizes the criteria, scoring, and selection rules of every reviewer, and Sec. lists the full prompts of all agents. The correspondence among panels, script clips, storyboard panels, and video clips (Sec. 3.1) is illustrated in Fig. A1. We further provide an HTML page in the supplementary material showcasing our generated videos.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: Figure A1: Correspondence among intermediate representations. Each manga panel (left) corresponds to one clip in the animation script (middle), which describes the environment, character positions, actions, and expressions of that panel in structured JSON format. Each script clip is then rendered as one storyboard panel (right). In first-frame mode, that panel conditions the corresponding video clip directly; in reference-conditioned mode, the complete storyboard jointly conditions the multi-shot video. Models. The Character Description Creator, Script Creator, Character Reviewer, Clip Reviewer, Storyboard Reviewer, and open-source Panel Reviewer use gemini-3.7-flash with the thinking level set to HIGH; the Video Reviewer uses gemini-3.1-pro-preview. The closed-source Storyboard Creator uses gemini-3.1-flash-image and outputs 16:9 storyboard at 1376 768 in 3 2 grid. We keep the default sampling parameters, including temperature, for all Gemini calls. Panel detection, reading-order estimation, and OCR use MAGI (Sachdeva & Zisserman, 2024). The open-source Storyboard Creator uses FLUX.2-dev with 28 inference steps and guidance scale of 4.0. It generates three candidates per panel at 768 640, and its panel reviewer, also gemini-3.7-flash, scores each candidate independently and keeps the highest-scoring one per panel. All experiments use = 2 refinement rounds, Ns = 3, Nb = 3, and Nv = 2. Video generation. In the reference-conditioned mode, the video model receives the complete best script as text prompt and the full storyboard grid as single reference image. The closed-source pipeline uses Seedance 2.0 (dreamina-seedance-2-0-260128) in this mode and produces 15 videos at 1280 720 and 24 fps, with generated audio. The open-source video-generation configuration supports two video backends. MiniMax-H3 (Ref2VA) runs in the same reference-conditioned mode and produces 15 videos at 1344 768 and 24 fps with audio. Index-AniSora V3.2 (Jiang et al., 2024) runs in the first-frame mode: each cropped storyboard panel is placed as the first frame of its clip, and each clip has 81 frames at 16 fps and 1280 720. Cropped panels are passed to the video model without resizing or padding, and any aspect-ratio adaptation is handled by the video models own preprocessing. In all cases, two candidate videos are generated and the Video Reviewer 16 Preprint. Under review. selects the better one; when the reviewer judges the two candidates comparable, the first candidate is kept. All main quantitative comparisons in Table 1 use the reference-conditioned mode; Table A5 separately compares the reference-conditioned and first-frame modes. Hardware and cost. Gemini and Seedance calls go through hosted APIs. MAGI runs locally on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB). FLUX.2-dev runs on an NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe, MiniMaxH3 on two NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (96 GB) GPUs, and Index-AniSora V3.2 on single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (96 GB). For each story, the closed-source pipeline makes 34.5 calls on average in the script and storyboard stages (28.5 Gemini text calls and 6 image-generation calls) and 3 in the video stage (2 Seedance generations and 1 Gemini review), costing about US$5.65 per story in total, of which US$4.55 is Seedance. The costs in Table A1 cover the script and storyboard stages, whereas the VLM calls and time in Table 1 are counted end-to-end, covering script generation, storyboard generation, video generation, and all reviews, and Calls (Video Gen) counts video-generation calls only. For locally run image and video backends, no external generation API calls are required, although the creator and reviewer agents still use Gemini APIs. Their local computational cost is reflected in the reported wall-clock time. Wall-clock times depend on hardware, parallelism, and API latency and should be regarded as indicative. OPEN-SOURCE STORYBOARD BACKEND In our experiments, the open-source image model we tested (FLUX.2-dev) did not reliably generate complete, high-quality multi-panel storyboard in single pass. We therefore adopt panel-wise generation strategy, producing multiple candidates for each panel and selecting the best one before composing the final storyboard. For each panel in the selected script, we construct prompt that incorporates the character descriptions, the corresponding script content, and constraints derived from the original manga panel to preserve its composition, camera viewpoint, and character pose. When character reference crops are available, they are explicitly associated with the corresponding characters during generation. FLUX.2-dev is conditioned on the source manga panel and the available character references to generate multiple candidates for each panel. Gemini-based reviewer then scores each candidate independently on manga/script follow (the primary criterion), character identity consistency, art style and colorization quality, and background fidelity, each on 04 scale, and the highest-scoring candidate is retained. The selected panels are then assembled into 3 2 storyboard grid, following the same output format as the closed-source backend to enable evaluation under unified protocol. Since every panel is conditioned on its source manga panel and the shared character references, these common conditions help maintain cross-panel consistency.

sections.title: C STORYBOARD QUANTITATIVE EVALUATION
sections.content: Evaluation metrics. We evaluate storyboards with CSD, CIDS, PA, and OCCM from ViStoryBench (Zhuang et al., 2026), adapting three of them to manga: CIDS uses SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) instead of CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) for finer character-crop detail, OCCMs expected character count comes from the source manga panel rather than the scripts cast list, and PA is judged by GPT-4.1 instead of Gemini (our pipelines reviewer) to reduce self-preference bias. Since all script-conditioned methods share the same refined script, PA measures content adherence under an identical specification, while CSD, CIDS, and OCCM (and the Manga Plot criterion of our user study) capture fidelity to the source manga itself; full definitions are in Appendix F. For Aesthetic Quality, we replace ViStoryBenchs general-purpose predictor with two anime-specific models, Aesthetic Shadow v21 and Waifu-v32, trained on anime/illustration imagery and used for training-data curation in production anime models. 1Released by shadowlilac as shadowlilac/aesthetic-shadow-v2, which is no longer available; we use the community mirror at https://huggingface.co/NeoChen1024/aesthetic-shadow-v2-backup. 2https://huggingface.co/Eugeoter/waifu-scorer-v3 17 Preprint. Table A1 compares storyboard generation across methods. The two Manga2Animate configurations jointly achieve the best results on all four manga-fidelity metrics: the open-source FLUX.2 backend reaches the highest CSD and OCCM, while the closed-source Gemini backend achieves the highest CIDS and PA, each improving over the best baseline. Since all baselines use the same refined script as our method, the PA gap reflects content adherence under an identical specification, and this advantage holds for both an open and closed image backend rather than relying on specific image model. In contrast, StoryDiffusion and Story-Iter score higher on the anime-specific aesthetic metrics but considerably lower on manga fidelity (CIDS, PA, OCCM), since both freely generate imagery from text without being constrained by the original characters and composition. This indicates that singleimage aesthetics and adaptation fidelity are distinct aspects: an aesthetic predictor assesses the appeal of an individual illustration without considering whether it is consistent with the source. The strengths of Manga2Animate lie in character preservation, content alignment, and cross-panel consistency, which matter most for this task, and participants in our user study also clearly preferred our results overall (Sec. 4.6). The two backends offer different cost trade-offs: FLUX.2 avoids external image-generation APIs but takes 1 59 min on local GPUs, while Gemini takes 20 min 2 with 6 image-generation calls. Both are slower than StoryDiffusion and AnyStory but considerably cheaper than AniMaker, another multi-agent pipeline (8 9 min); users can choose backend according to their compute resources and API budget.

sections.title: D ADDITIONAL ABLATION RESULTS
sections.content: Script selection strategy. Sec. 4.7 compares clip-wise and script-wise script selection and reports the headline result; Table A2 gives the full metric breakdown. Clip-wise selection outperforms script-wise selection on I2VS, Subject Consistency, Background Consistency, and both aesthetic metrics, raising Waifu-v3 from 4.423 to 5.090 and Shadow-v2 from 0.473 to 0.518, while DD increases from 5.951 to 9.457. I2VB and Motion Smoothness are slightly lower than with script-wise selection (0.768 vs. 0.772 and 0.960 vs. 0.963), with both gaps within 0.004. We conjecture that clip-wise selection retains the more complete and specific clip descriptions among the candidates, enabling the video model to produce richer motion and visuals, whereas combining descriptions from different candidates may introduce slight variations in scene settings, causing the small drop in I2VB. sections.title: E BASELINE ADAPTATION
sections.content: StoryDiffusion (storyboard). StoryDiffusions official multi-character mechanism takes only plain-text, per-shot prompts that tag which characters appear, with no interface for imageconditioned identity. To keep the comparison fair, we take the same final best script produced by Manga2Animates own creator-reviewer refinement (Sec. 3.4) and reformat character descriptions and per-shot scene/action text into the per-shot prompts its official multi-character mechanism requires. Because StoryDiffusion has no reference-image input, the manga-cropped character images used elsewhere in our evaluation do not apply here; identity relies purely on text description, limitation of the method when processing image information. Each story yields 6 panels, composed into the same 3 2 grid as the other backends for evaluation. Story-Iter (storyboard). Story-Iter generates sequence of story images from ordered text prompts and maintains cross-image consistency through Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA) over previously generated results. To unify the story content, we convert the final refined script of Manga2Animate (Sec. 3.4) into six prompts ordered by manga panel, preserving the characters, interactions, scenes, actions, and camera descriptions. Generation follows the official settings with the comic style. Since Story-Iter does not accept external character reference images, we do not add an identity-control module. The six generated images are composed into 3 2 grid in order and scored with MangaEval. AnyStory (storyboard). AnyStory supports personalized story image generation with character reference images. To unify the story content, we convert the final refined script of Manga2Animate (Sec. 3.4) into the structured script required by AnyStory, preserving the characters, scenes, actions, interactions, and camera descriptions of the six panels, and we use the same manga-cropped character images as character references. All other stages follow the official AnyStory implementation, without adding the Storyboard Creator or Reviewer of Manga2Animate. The six generated images are composed into 3 2 grid in panel order and scored with MangaEval. AniMaker (video). AniMaker natively takes plain-text story and self-generates both the script (via an LLM) and the character portrait (via Hunyuan3D (Zhao et al., 2025)). To compare videogeneration ability rather than manga-understanding ability, we replace only these two front-end stages: the script is converted from Manga2Animates own final, refined script (Sec. 3.4) into AniMakers native script.json format, and the character portrait is replaced with the same mangacropped reference image used by our pipeline. All remaining stages (environment-image generation, scene-prompt synthesis, MCTS-based candidate clip generation and selection, narration, and final 20 Preprint. Under review. assembly) retain AniMakers original implementation and default hyperparameters, and outputs are scored under the same MangaEval protocol as all baselines. StoryMem (video). StoryMem generates multi-shot videos shot by shot from structured story script and visual memory. To unify the story content, we convert the final refined script of Manga2Animate (Sec. 3.4) into the StoryMem format, preserving the characters, actions, scenes, and camera descriptions, and adopt the reference-initialized M2V setting, which uses the six manga panels as the initial visual references. Video generation uses the Wan2.2-I2V-A14B (Wan et al., 2025) backbone with the corresponding StoryMem LoRA checkpoint, and the visual-memory update and shot-by-shot generation follow the official settings. We keep its original mechanism without adding the storyboard, Video Reviewer, or candidate selection of Manga2Animate, and the generated shots are concatenated in script order for evaluation. ViMax (video). ViMax supports screenplay as input and automatically performs storyboarding, shot planning, character image generation, and video clip generation. To prevent it from rewriting the story from short concept, we use its Script2Video workflow and convert the final refined script of Manga2Animate (Sec. 3.4) into screenplay input that preserves the characters, scenes, actions, dialogue, camera descriptions, and narrative order. The manga-cropped character images serve as ViMaxs character references to maintain appearance consistency. We use gemini-3.6-flash and gemini-3.1-flash-image as the language and image generation models, and Seedance 2.0 (or Veo 3.1 Fast) as the video generation model through external APIs. All other storyboard, shot-planning, and video-generation stages follow the original Script2Video pipeline of ViMax, without adding the storyboard or reviewer modules of Manga2Animate.

sections.content: We provide full definitions for the metrics summarized in Tables A6 and A7. 21 Preprint. Under review. Storyboard level. Visual Consistency is measured by CSD and CIDS, each reporting the average of cross score (similarity between generated panels and the character reference images) and self score (similarity among generated panels). CSD (Somepalli et al., 2024) uses CSD-CLIP ViT-L style features and is unmodified. CIDS detects characters in the generated panels with GroundingDINO (Liu et al., 2024b), assigns them to reference characters by Hungarian matching (Kuhn, 1955), and compares identity features; we replace the original CLIP at 224px with SigLIP (so400m) at 384px, and the cross score is computed over successfully matched character crops. Content Alignment is measured by PA and OCCM. PA uses GPT-4.1 to score each panel on scene, character action, and camera, and each character crop on single-character action, on 04 scale; each item is sampled 5 times at temperature 1.0 and averaged, and PA is the average over the four aspects. The scoring reference is the per-panel text converted from the refined script, which is shared by all (cid:16) script-conditioned methods. OCCM = 100 exp , where is the number of characters GroundingDINO detects in the generated panel and is the expected count, now obtained by applying the same detector to the source manga panel rather than taken from the scripts cast list. Aesthetic Quality is measured by two anime-specific models: Aesthetic Shadow v2 (a 1.1Bparameter high-/low-quality ViT classifier, score = (high quality)) and Waifu-Scorer v3 (CLIP ViT-L/14 features with an MLP regression head, output in [0, 10]), averaged over the six generated panels. Computational Cost is the average number of VLM/LLM calls, image-generation calls, and wall-clock time per story. DE ϵ+max(E,1) (cid:17) Video level. Each video is split into six segments corresponding to the six manga panels, and metrics are computed per segment and averaged. Manga Alignment is measured by I2VS and I2VB. I2VS measures the subject similarity between the frames of each segment and the corresponding character reference image using VBench++s original formula, which combines the maximum similarity to the reference with the mean and minimum similarity between consecutive frames, with its DINO ViT-B/16 backbone replaced by DINOv3 ViT-B/16; segments without characters are excluded. I2VB measures the background similarity between the frames of each segment and the corresponding source manga panel using DreamSim (Fu et al., 2023) features, with both formula and backbone unmodified. Video Quality is measured by Subject Consistency and Background Consistency (DINOand CLIP-based frame-to-first-frame and frame-to-previous-frame similarity, respectively, both unmodified VBench++ metrics), Motion Smoothness (an unmodified VBench++ metric based on AMT frame interpolation (Li et al., 2023)), and Dynamic Degree. We change DD from VBench++s binary decision based on the top-5% RAFT (Teed & Deng, 2020) flow magnitudes into continuous motion-magnitude score: each video is resampled to about 8 fps, RAFT computes optical flow between consecutive frames at the native resolution, and the flow magnitude is averaged over all pixels and frame pairs and normalized by 256/ min(H, ). DD measures motion magnitude rather than motion correctness. Aesthetic Quality reuses Aesthetic Shadow v2 and Waifu-Scorer v3 from the storyboard level, applied to every frame per video and averaged. Computational Cost is the end-to-end average number of VLM calls, generation calls, and wall-clock time per story.

sections.title: G REVIEWER CRITERIA
sections.content: All reviewers are prompted to first describe each candidate with respect to every criterion before reaching verdict, and to output structured JSON object containing per-criterion winners or scores, an overall winner, and improvement suggestions for the winner. The suggestions include only criteria on which the winner still shows observable weaknesses and serve as the feedback passed to the next refinement round. The full prompts are listed in Appendix H. Character Reviewer. Inputs: the ordered manga panels, the character reference image(s), and the character descriptions of all Ns candidate scripts. Criteria (one winner each, one point per win): (1) clothing match, (2) physical appearance accuracy, including facial features, hairstyle, and body proportions, (3) color accuracy with respect to the character reference image, and (4) left/right specificity of asymmetric features such as scars, hair parts, and accessories. The manga panels serve as the ground truth except for colors, which follow the reference image. Ties in total score are broken in the priority order (2) > (1) > (4) > (3). 22 Preprint. Under review. Clip Reviewer. Inputs: one manga panel, the character descriptions (used only to identify characters), and the Ns candidate descriptions of that panel. Criteria (one winner each): (1) small objects associated with each character, penalizing both missing and hallucinated objects, (2) facial expressions and emotions, (3) background accuracy, (4) object placement and orientation, (5) character body orientation and spatial relationships, and (6) dialogue speaker assignment. Ties are broken in the priority order (6) > (5) > (4) > (2) > (1) > (3). The reviewer runs independently for each panel position, and the winning descriptions are reassembled into the final script  (Fig. 4)  . Storyboard Reviewer. Inputs: the six manga panels, the character reference image(s), two candidate storyboards and B, and the script used to generate them. Thirteen criteria, one point each: (1) character identity preservation, (2) overall art-style consistency with the manga, (3) color presence (not primarily black-and-white), (4) consistent panel size in the 3 2 layout, (5) only existing characters, (6) narrative order consistency, (7) script alignment, (8) rich background, (9) background consistency across panels, (10) character and object position consistency across panels, (11) panelinternal object layout match with the manga, (12) no dialogue boxes or captions, and (13) left/right consistency of asymmetric character features. Criteria (3), (4), (5), (6), and (12) are judged pass/- fail for each storyboard independently, so both storyboards may receive the point; the others are comparative. The storyboard with the higher total wins, and remaining ties are broken by fixed criterion priority order. From the second round onward, variant of the prompt compares each new candidate with the previous best storyboard, each judged against the script it was generated from. Open-source panel reviewer. Inputs: the source manga panel, the character references for that panel (possibly none), the corresponding script clip, and one candidate panel. Each candidate is scored independently on 04 scale for (1) manga/script follow, covering action, pose, composition, and framing (the primary criterion), (2) character identity consistency, (3) art style and colorization quality, penalizing black-and-white line art, screentone residue, and speech bubbles, and (4) background and environment fidelity. The candidate with the highest total is kept, with ties broken by criterion (1). Video Reviewer. Inputs: the generation prompt and two candidate videos and B, plus the previously selected clip for every clip after the first in the first-frame mode. For the first clip, and in the reference-conditioned mode, the criteria and weights are visual realism (0.35), physical commonsense (0.30), and video-prompt alignment (0.35), where alignment also checks left/right directional correctness. For subsequent clips in the first-frame mode, these weights become 0.2 each, and coherency with the previous clip is added with weight of 0.4. Each criterion is scored 1 (A wins), 0 (B wins), or 0.5 (tie), and penalty of 0.5 is subtracted for violating hard constraints, such as sudden appearance or disappearance of main objects, unnecessary scene transitions, or unnaturally fast or slow motion. If the weighted scores differ by less than 0.05, the two candidates are judged comparable and the first candidate is kept. 23 Preprint. Under review.
